text_blocks.snippet: The most effective method to regain your sense of smell after COVID is olfactory training, which involves repeatedly smelling specific scents to stimulate and retrain the olfactory nerves. This method aims to rebuild the connections between the nose and the brain's smell-processing center.

list.title: Choose scents:
list.snippet: Select four distinct and strong scents, such as lemon, eucalyptus, rose, or clove.

list.title: Smell each scent:
list.snippet: For 25 seconds, deeply inhale each scent, focusing on recalling associated memories and feelings.

list.title: Rest:
list.snippet: Allow a minute for your brain to process each scent before moving to the next.

list.title: Repeat:
list.snippet: Perform this exercise twice daily (morning and night) for several months.

text_blocks.snippet: While olfactory training can be a helpful tool, it's important to consult with a healthcare professional for personalized advice and to rule out any other underlying causes of smell loss.

text_blocks.snippet: To help regain your sense of smell after COVID, olfactory training (smell training) can be beneficial. This involves repeatedly smelling specific scents, such as essential oils or common household items, and consciously connecting them with memories and mental images.
snippet_highlighted_words: olfactory training (smell training) can be beneficial

text_blocks.snippet: Here's how olfactory training can be done:

list.snippet: Choose your scents: Select 4 distinct scents, like lemon, oregano, eucalyptus, and rose.
Smell each scent for 25 seconds: Take gentle whiffs of each scent, focusing on recalling what the smell is like, what it feels like, and any memories associated with it.
Allow for mental processing: Give your brain a minute to process each scent before moving on to the next.
Repeat twice a day: Perform this exercise morning and night for about three months.

text_blocks.snippet: Why it works: Olfactory training helps stimulate the nerve cells in your nose and can help your brain re-establish connections with specific scents, as smell and memory are closely linked.

list.snippet: Give it time: It may take time for your sense of smell to fully return, so be patient.
Consider restoring nerve function: In some cases, restoring nerve function may also be necessary.
Consult with a healthcare professional: If you have concerns or if your sense of smell doesn't improve, consult with a doctor or ENT specialist.
